title: Visual Space Perception and Visually Directed Action
research_question: Do natural environments viewed binocularly from a stationary vantage point lead to veridical perception, and how do systematic distortions in visual space perception (matching tasks) relate to accuracy in visually directed action (walking/pointing tasks)?

participants.description: Experiment 1: 10 male students (20-33 years) from University of São Paulo, 20/20 vision, active nonprofessional players. Experiment 2: 10 male students (18-33 years) from University of São Paulo. Experiment 3: 5 graduate students (24-29 years) from University of California, Santa Barbara.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: White steel rods (16 cm high, 1 cm diameter) used as targets. Experiments 1 & 2 conducted on a grassy field (35m x 20m) with a 1m grid. Experiment 3 conducted in a lightproof warehouse (35m x 20m) with a 1200cm square workspace and a red neon lamp at the center. Paths for walking were marked on the ground.

measures.instrument: Method of adjustment (subjects commanded assistants to place targets)
Measurement of physical distance walked by subjects with eyes closed

measures.construct: Continuous pointing direction to unseen target
measures.instrument: Measurement of arm orientation using a video system while subjects walked with eyes closed
Calculated as difference between walked distance and physical target distance
Calculated from pointing direction relative to target azimuth

findings.consequent: perceived length relative to frontal intervals
findings.mechanism: Perceptual foreshortening of depth intervals relative to frontal intervals.
findings.quote: the depth intervals had to be made much larger in order to be judged equal to the width intervals

findings.consequent: perceptual foreshortening of depth intervals (ratio of matched depth to frontal interval)
findings.mechanism: The degree of perceptual foreshortening increases with distance from the observer.
findings.quote: The ratio of depth to width increased with egocentric distance

findings.consequent: perceptual foreshortening of depth intervals (ratio of matched depth to frontal interval)
findings.mechanism: The degree of perceptual foreshortening increases with the length of the interval.
findings.quote: The ratio also increased with interval length

findings.consequent: mean signed distance error in walking
findings.mechanism: A slight average overshoot in walked distance to single targets.
findings.quote: The mean signed distance error for all subjects and targets was 55 cm indicating an overshoot on average

findings.mechanism: Walked distance to single targets was near-linear with physical distance, indicating high accuracy.
findings.quote: The dotted line shows what perfectly accurate responding would have been.

findings.consequent: perceived length relative to frontal intervals
findings.mechanism: Replication of Experiment 1 matching task results, showing depth intervals had to be made larger to appear equal, with the increase in ratio more apparent for all three interval lengths.
findings.quote: The results are very much like those in Figure 3a, except that the increase in ratio with egocentric distance was more apparent for all three interval lengths.

findings.antecedent: previously viewed first target location (width condition)
findings.consequent: mean signed distance error in walking
findings.mechanism: A mean undershoot of 27 cm when walking to the first target in the width condition.
findings.quote: In the width condition, the mean signed error was -27 cm (undershoot)

findings.antecedent: previously viewed first target location (depth condition)
findings.consequent: mean signed distance error in walking
findings.mechanism: A mean undershoot of 50 cm when walking to the first target in the depth condition.
findings.quote: in the depth condition, the mean signed error was -50 cm (undershoot)

findings.mechanism: Walked distances to the first target were near-linear with physical distance in both width and depth conditions (power function exponents 0.98 and 0.96).
findings.quote: The corresponding power function exponents were .98 and .96, indicating near-linearity of the responses.

findings.mechanism: Mean walked intervals between two targets were overestimated by about 50 cm compared to physical intervals.
findings.quote: the mean intervals were on the average about 50 cm larger than the corresponding physical intervals

findings.mechanism: Despite perceptual foreshortening in matching tasks, walking to two targets did not manifest this anisotropy (ratio of width response to depth response was near 1.0), except for some anisotropy in the reverse direction for the smallest interval size.
findings.quote: walking to two targets does not manifest this anisotropy, although there is some anisotropy in the reverse direction for the smallest interval size.

findings.consequent: continuous blind pointing direction while walking
findings.mechanism: Subjects accurately pointed to an unseen target while walking, indicating correct perception of egocentric distance and imaginal updating.
findings.quote: the mean pointing direction nearly coincides with that of the target for all three paths

findings.consequent: angular velocity of arm during continuous pointing
findings.mechanism: The systematic change in arm angular velocity during pointing suggests continuous imaginal updating of target location rather than preprogrammed arm rotation.
findings.quote: the angular velocity of the arm...changes systematically during the traverse in accord with the true target azimuth.

mechanisms: Dissociation between perceived egocentric distance and perceived exocentric distance
Cognitive correction of misperceived distance (conscious or unconscious learning)
Separation of visual systems for conscious perception and motor control (two visual systems)
Imaginal updating of an internal spatial representation during locomotion
limitations: Reliance on scale construction methods using judgments of exocentric distance may cast doubt on validity.
Direct scaling measures of perceived distance may be contaminated by cognitive correction.
Uncertainty about the purity of measures obtained with 'apparent' instructions without independent evaluation.
Comparability issues between matching tasks (exocentric intervals) and walking tasks (absolute locations).
Reduced cue availability in darkened rooms may lead to underestimation of target distance (referencing other studies).
Verbal responses in other studies may yield different results than motoric responses used here.
